R_H1.passageTitle: Many Kinds of Work at CERN

passages.label: A
passages.text: Who helps set up an experiment before anyone can look at a result? CERN employs people in many different fields. Its careers site lists physics, engineering and campus services, and it also introduces applicants to support work. A person who wants to apply can look at each department and learn what people do there. One scientific workplace can contain more than one occupation.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Work with people appears in human resources and communication. CERN says its human-resources team helps create an inclusive environment where different people feel welcome. Communication staff build public, political, and financial support for CERN's mission. A manager or employee in these areas spends time listening, explaining, and solving problems. A colleague is part of a wider team that connects support staff with scientists and engineers. Such work suits someone who enjoys helping and talking, although it also needs careful planning. A team may advertise a job and ask how people learned to work with others.

passages.label: C
passages.text: In other jobs, people work with facts and records. One group looks at data to find out what the research has shown. A group that deals with money checks where the money goes. Other staff help people make plans, keep records or work out what a task will cost. These jobs use information in different ways. Someone might like finding a pattern in a set of numbers or keeping the records clear enough for a team to know what comes next. These are some of the ways employees run everyday services. An advertisement that a team uses to advertise a role can tell students which activity a particular section does every day.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Other jobs are about making things work. People working on an electrical project may set up equipment, look at a drawing to find out how a part fits and write down what happens. A team can run out of spare parts, and a careless mistake could waste time, so a workshop may keep tools in a separate section. The people who hire new workers look for the skill needed to do each job safely.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Some physicists begin with a theory and organise a test to see how well it works. Some colleagues turn the result into words the public can understand. In an office a manager may have a different goal, such as helping people run a project on time. A student can use a hobby as a clue to what kind of work to explore and ask for advice about where to look next.

questions.prompt: What role can an activity someone enjoys play when thinking about work?
options: It can give them a starting point for learning about a job.
It shows which department must employ them.
It is enough by itself to settle which job will fit.

passages.label: A
passages.text: A short quiz can begin a career conversation, but a real assessment often asks more questions, and the O*NET Interest Profiler is a public career-exploration tool developed for the United States Department of Labor. Its current web version has 30 questions, while a paper short form has 60, and people can complete it online. The tool asks which work activities a person might enjoy, then connects the answers with more than one occupation.

passages.label: B
passages.text: O*NET distinguishes six interests. Realistic refers to practical, hands-on work. People with an Investigative interest like finding facts and solving problems. Artistic work involves creating or designing. Social means that people like to teach or help others. Enterprising concerns leading or making decisions, and a Conventional interest often shows itself in work with rules, details and data.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Everyday choices can provide clues, and a person can write down a skill they use well, a strength they want to develop and a weakness they might need help with, and it may help to spend time on a small project to see how the work feels. For a new occupation, find out who would hire you and how you would earn money, as well as which tasks can cause stress. There may be another section of work that offers a better match.

passages.label: D
passages.text: After the questions, the user receives a score for each interest, and the result can suggest careers from a collection of over 900 O*NET occupations. On My Next Move, career pages also show preparation levels and details about the work, and a student can open one section, compare a number of careers, and organise further research. This turns a broad preference into names that a learner can investigate, compare, and discuss with an adult, and a high score does not promise that every suggested job will suit the person. Education, ability, values, and local opportunities still matter, and a familiar job title can be a starting point. The suggested occupations can also include jobs a student has never seen before.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Use the results to explore work. Look at a listing where a company advertises an occupation. Check which department employs people in that role and how to apply. An office visit can introduce a student to an employee or a manager. Ask how colleagues organise their day. A teacher can give advice on a goal for the next visit. A career report makes a useful start when it leads to a question someone can follow up.

R_H3.passageTitle: Using AI to Warn About River Floods

passages.label: A
passages.text: A flood warning can reach a local office before river water reaches the road. Some places have little data on river levels, which makes warnings difficult. In 2018 Google began a pilot in India to test forecasts of river floods. Its goal was to give people time to prepare. The project brought employees and colleagues from research teams into contact with people who understood rivers and warning systems.

passages.label: B
passages.text: A flood forecasting product does not answer questions like a chatbot. It uses patterns in information to forecast floods. To run its computer models, programs that represent real-world processes, Google uses weather forecasts and satellite images taken from space that are open to the public. Its system combines two models. One estimates how much water will flow in a river. The other estimates which areas could be covered by water and how deep it might become. A forecast is a possible result based on available information, not a promise that events will happen exactly as predicted.

passages.label: C
passages.text: In 2022, Google introduced Flood Hub to organise flood forecasts. The platform displays the information on a map. The Centre for Humanitarian Data later became a partner in this work. The company first offered the platform in 20 countries. In May 2023, Google announced an expansion to 80 countries, including places in Africa, Asia, Europe and the Americas. The forecasts covered areas where about 460 million people lived. At that time, some forecasts looked as far as seven days ahead. A longer warning can give individuals and organisations more time to consider their next steps.

passages.label: D
passages.text: The forecast depends on a project with universities, governments and aid organisations. Staff may set up ways to share local reports and write down what a model predicted before a flood. Then they can look at records to find out where a forecast worked and which weakness needs attention. Local skill matters, particularly when towns run out of time to alert residents. A careless interpretation could also put stress on staff who need to decide what information to send.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Researchers need to check how well the model works. A team reported tests in 2024 that it had set up to compare its forecasts with an existing system. Where the data did not allow a full check, Google gave researchers an extra section of forecasts. Local departments can apply such evidence to decisions about how to prepare. The product gives an office new information, while a manager may still need advice on what those results mean for a particular place.
